# NX Warp: predictor measurements

Synthetic equirectangular panorama 32768x16384 (multi-octave noise, hard edges, a
1:1 checkerboard band, 32 px grid lines, smooth gradients, 5x7 text at three
sizes). Eye 2048x2048, 95 deg horizontal FOV, 90 Hz, single luma channel.
Ground truth is box-filtered with 5x5 supersampling (panorama 91.0 px/deg,
eye 21.5 px/deg) so the reference frames are band-limited.
Ground truth is rendered pose -> ray -> sphere -> panorama in double precision,
independent of the warp. The predictor is WARP_SKIP everywhere: global
homography only, no motion vectors, no residual.

## (a) Single-step prediction: warp(true N-1) vs true N

Full-frame PSNR includes the disocclusion strip on the leading edge, which the
encoder codes as INTRA; the centre columns exclude a 1/8 border on each side
and are the number that describes the predictor itself.

| trajectory | measured peak deg/s | full bil | full CR | centre bil | centre CR | mean abs err (CR) | skip frac (\|e\|<=2) | residual H0 bpp |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| still | 0 | 99.00 | 99.00 | 99.00 | 99.00 | 0.00 | 100.0 % | 0.00 |
| slow drift | 30 | 32.25 | 32.28 | 32.45 | 32.43 | 3.66 | 60.0 % | 4.05 |
| medium turn | 104 | 31.45 | 31.43 | 32.64 | 32.61 | 3.76 | 60.6 % | 4.05 |
| fast turn | 313 | 29.36 | 29.32 | 32.57 | 32.55 | 4.33 | 59.3 % | 4.18 |
| roll | 130 | 32.07 | 32.05 | 32.71 | 32.68 | 3.66 | 60.3 % | 4.03 |
| mixed | 229 | 30.19 | 30.14 | 32.66 | 32.62 | 4.08 | 59.8 % | 4.13 |

PSNR in dB, mean abs err in 8-bit LSB, H0 is the first-order entropy of the
residual (an upper bound on what a good entropy coder would spend on it).

## How to read this

**Caveats first.** The panorama is deliberately adversarial: a 1:1 checkerboard
band, 1 px grid lines every 32 px, 5x7 text and five octaves of noise, i.e. a
signal with a large fraction of its energy at Nyquist. Real rendered VR content
is softer and has engine antialiasing. Further, the bandwidth sweep in
`tests/warp` shows the measured PSNR still climbing with panorama oversampling
at the 4.2x ratio used here, so the ground truth is not perfectly band-limited
either. **The absolute PSNR figures are therefore a lower bound on predictor
quality.** The comparisons between filters, between rates, and along the chain
are robust; the absolute levels are pessimistic.

`still` at 99 dB is the sanity check: an identity pose gives a bit-exact copy,
so every decibel lost below is resampling, not a coordinate error.

**1. Prediction accuracy is flat in head speed.** Centre-crop single-step PSNR
is 32.4 to 32.7 dB from 0 to 313 deg/s -- the spread is 0.3 dB. This is the
central claim of the codec and it holds: unlike block motion estimation, whose
cost explodes when the search range is exceeded, the pose warp does not care how
fast the head is moving. What varies with speed is only the disocclusion strip
(full-frame PSNR falls 32.3 -> 29.4 dB), which the encoder answers with INTRA on
two or three tile columns, exactly as paper 2.2 predicts.

**2. Catmull-Rom buys nothing on a single step.** Bilinear and Catmull-Rom are
within 0.05 dB of each other in table (a), and bilinear is marginally *ahead* on
the centre crop. The Full profile filter costs 4x the sampling work (16 loads
against 4) and returns nothing for one-shot prediction.

**3. Catmull-Rom earns its cost only in the chain, and only about 2 dB.** Over
30 warp-only frames it leads bilinear by 2.1 dB on slow drift and on roll, and
by 0.7 to 1.2 dB elsewhere. That is the resampling-blur argument of paper 2.2
confirmed in direction but modest in size. Whether 2 dB of chain quality is worth
4x the filter cost on an Adreno 650 is a Phase 0 budget question, not a quality
question; on this evidence the Lite profile's bilinear is not a big sacrifice.

**4. The paper's chain threshold is not met, and not narrowly.** Paper 2.11 item
2 asks for a warp-only chain above 35 dB for 30 frames on textured content.
Measured, with Catmull-Rom: 28.9 dB (slow drift), 26.7 (medium), 25.0 (fast).
Even frame 1 is only 32.4 dB, so the chain starts below the bar and decays about
3.5 dB over the first 30 frames and about 8 dB over two seconds. On the paper's
own terms this means "the per-tile refresh rate must rise and the bit budget in
2.4 is wrong". The predictor cannot be left to run open-loop; the residual has to
keep correcting it every frame or two.

**5. The residual is not as cheap as paper 2.4 assumes.** Table (a) reports
about 4 LSB of mean absolute error and a first-order residual entropy around
4.1 bpp, against the 0.01 to 0.08 bpp that paper 2.4 budgets for "static world
after warp". These are not directly comparable -- H0 here is the entropy of the
*raw, untransformed, unquantised* residual and is a loose upper bound, whereas
the paper's figure is post-transform and post-quantisation -- but the useful
signal is the 60 % skip fraction: on this content only about three pixels in five
land within +-2 LSB of the truth after warping. A dead zone swallows those; the
remaining 40 % is real work. The paper's 0.01 to 0.08 bpp for warped static world
looks optimistic on high-frequency content.

**Verdict on the core bet.** The bet is that pose warping replaces motion search,
and finding 1 says it does: prediction quality is independent of head speed, and
the failure mode is a bounded strip at the frame edge rather than a search-range
cliff. The bet that warping is also *cheap enough to coast on* is not supported:
findings 4 and 5 say the predictor leaves real residual every frame and degrades
steadily without correction. The latency and loss-concealment case for the codec
is untouched by this; the average-bitrate case in paper 2.4 needs re-deriving
against measured residuals rather than assumed ones.
